usage: xo debug [--batch] [--json] [--timeout=DUR] [-c CMD]... PROG [ARGS]
       xo debug -p PID [--batch] [--json] [--timeout=DUR] [-c CMD]... PROG
       xo debug --dap

Runs PROG, a native executable with its debug information (a native
build keeps it unless -s or --release), under xo's own debugger
(decision 0253) with ARGS. The commands come from -c, in order (--batch
requires them: each is echoed as `(xo) CMD`, then its output), else one a
line from standard input, with the prompt `(xo) ` on a terminal and an
empty line repeating the last command. --json prints one JSON line per
command instead (spec 11.5). The program is ended after the last command.
--timeout=DUR bounds each wait for the program's next stop (run, continue,
step, next, finish): with no stop within DUR the program is ended (an
attached one detached and left running) and the command says so, so a
script or an agent never waits forever.
-p PID attaches to the running process PID instead (PROG its executable:
its debug information): every thread is stopped, and quit detaches,
leaving it running; for a hung program, tasks shows what each task waits
on. --dap serves the Debug Adapter Protocol on standard input and output for
an editor (VS Code, Zed, nvim-dap): the editor's launch request names the
program (decision 0504).

Commands: break (b) FILE:LINE or FUNCTION, delete N, run (r), continue
(c), step (s: to the next line, into calls), next (n: over calls), finish
(out of the selected frame, an inlined call's too), print (p)
NAME[.FIELD]..., locals, backtrace (bt), frame N, tasks, task N [bt],
threads, quit (q). A stop suspends every thread of the program; step and
next run the stopped thread alone, one instruction at a time, and a call
they step over with every thread. tasks lists the program's tasks from
the runtime's records, as xo dump does (what each is blocked in, and
where); task N selects a blocked task's frames (bt: and prints them).

macOS arm64, Linux and Windows amd64. On macOS xo needs the
com.apple.security.cs.debugger entitlement (ad hoc for development, the
release signature for a release) and Developer Mode
(DevToolsSecurity -enable). On Linux it uses ptrace (a security module
such as Yama's ptrace_scope may forbid it); -p is not built there yet.
On Windows it uses the system's debugging functions.

Example:
  xo build -o sum ./sum
  xo debug --batch -c 'b main.xo:9' -c run -c locals -c bt sum
